content: Premature birth, also referred to as preterm birth, occurs when a baby is delivered before the standard duration of pregnancy is completed. In most medical systems, prematurity is defined as the birth of an infant before 37 weeks of gestation, calculated from the first day of the mother’s last menstrual period (LMP). In contrast, postmature birth is defined as delivery occurring after 42 weeks of gestation. The typical length of a human pregnancy is 266 days, but for practical purposes, gestational age is often calculated from the LMP, with conception assumed to occur approximately 14 days after the LMP. This makes a full-term pregnancy approximately 280 days or 40 weeks in duration. Medically, preterm birth is defined as childbirth occurring before 37 completed weeks of pregnancy. In the United States, approximately 12% of infants, or 1 in 8, are born prematurely each year. For example, in 2003, over 490,000 babies in the U.S. were born preterm. Globally, determining rates of prematurity is more challenging due to limited access to professional obstetric care in many developing regions, which makes accurate assessment of gestational age less reliable. Instead, the World Health Organization (WHO) monitors rates of low birth weight, which affected 16.5% of births in less developed regions in 2000. It is estimated that one-third of these low birth weight cases are attributable to premature delivery. The shorter the duration of pregnancy, the higher the risk of complications for the infant. Prematurely born infants face an increased risk of death during their first year of life, with the majority of these deaths occurring within the first month (neonatal mortality). Globally, prematurity accounts for approximately 10% of neonatal deaths, equating to around 500,000 deaths annually. In the United States, where infections and other causes of neonatal death have been significantly reduced, prematurity is the leading cause of neonatal mortality, accounting for 25% of such deaths. Infants born prematurely are at heightened risk for a range of serious health complications. These include cerebral palsy, chronic lung disease, gastrointestinal disorders, intellectual disabilities, vision or hearing impairments, and an increased likelihood of developing depression during adolescence. Despite the identification of several risk factors for preterm birth, nearly half of all cases have no identifiable cause. When possible, medical professionals may attempt to halt premature labor to allow the pregnancy to progress closer to full term, thereby improving the infant’s chances of survival and long-term health. However, there is currently no universally effective method to prevent or stop preterm labor. Alarmingly, the rate of preterm births in the United States has risen by 30% over the past two decades. In developed countries, premature infants are typically cared for in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs). Physicians specializing in the care of critically ill or premature infants are known as neonatologists. Modern neonatal care involves advanced monitoring of vital parameters such as temperature, respiration, cardiac function, oxygen levels, and brain activity. Treatments may include intravenous fluids and nutrition, oxygen supplementation, mechanical ventilation, and medications. In contrast, in developing countries where access to advanced medical equipment and reliable electricity may be limited, simple interventions can significantly reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with prematurity. The term ex-premies is used to describe infants who were born prematurely, before reaching the standard 37 weeks of gestation.
